subsection: 2. Working hours, leisure time and conditions of work

notes.b: The standard working week has shortened over the last century, and regular overtime has become less common for many workers. This has changed how families divide their time, and the law now sets limits on how much an employee can be asked to work.
points: Working hours fell as the standard working week was shortened and regular overtime (extra paid hours beyond the normal week) became less common for many workers.

The Organisation of Working Time Act 1997 sets an average maximum working week of 48 hours, a minimum daily rest period, rest breaks during the working day, a weekly rest period, paid annual leave and public holiday entitlements.
Because these limits are set by Irish law, an employee cannot lawfully be required to work beyond them, which protects workers' health and their time with their families.

Part-time and flexible hours let some parents work around school hours and be at home earlier in the day. Other flexible arrangements include job-sharing, flexitime, term-time working, compressed hours, and remote and hybrid working.
The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 gives employees a right to request flexible and remote working, for example so they can care for a child or relative.
Shift work and extended opening hours in retail and services mean that some family members work evenings or weekends, so families must plan time together.

Shorter hours give families more time for shared meals, homework, household tasks and outings, and mean more time at home to care for children and for older relatives. They also bring a better work-life balance and less stress.
Not every effect is positive: long commuting and irregular hours cut time together, and technology means work can follow people home, for example emails received out of hours.
notes.tip: Hours did not fall for every family: with both parents now working, total family working hours can be higher than a century ago. Say 'average maximum' for the 48 hours, and give each effect a clear link to family life, not just a description.

notes.b: Shorter working hours and easier housework left families with more free time than earlier generations had. That free time changed what families do together, with benefits and some drawbacks.
points: Paid annual leave gives employees a set number of holiday weeks each year, which made family holidays a regular feature of family life.
Labour-saving appliances such as washing machines, dishwashers and microwaves, and convenience foods, cut the time spent on housework and cooking, releasing time for leisure.
Weekends became the main block of free time for most workers and their families.
Rising household incomes increased spending on leisure, including cinema, sport, holidays, travel and eating out.
Home entertainment such as television, radio, computers, the internet, streaming and gaming changed how families spend evenings, often indoors.
Community sport and clubs, such as GAA, soccer, swimming and dance, give children and parents structured leisure outside the home.
Shared activities strengthen family relationships and communication, support children's physical, social and emotional development, and relaxation reduces stress.
Leisure also has downsides: screen-based leisure can separate family members, and because leisure costs money, some families cannot afford it.
notes.tip: Keep to the effect of more free time on the family: a typical short question asks for two effects of more leisure time on a family. Give a reason or example with each, such as shared activities strengthening relationships.

notes.h: Improved pay: more income for families
notes.b: As the economy became more productive, pay rose, and the law now protects the lowest earners. Higher pay changes what a family can afford.
points: Real pay (pay after allowing for price rises) rose as productivity and living standards increased, giving families more disposable income to save, buy a home, and pay for education, holidays and leisure.
The National Minimum Wage Act 2000 sets a legal minimum hourly rate of pay, protecting low-paid workers and their families.
The Payment of Wages Act 1991 sets the rules on how wages must be paid and on what deductions an employer may make.
Higher incomes let families move to larger or better housing, buy household goods and build savings, and financial security reduces stress and arguments in the home.
Better pay and the cost of housing mean many families now need two incomes, which links to the growth in women's paid work.
notes.tip: Improved conditions came mainly from legislation and trade unions, not employers' generosity, so name the Act or the union for each improvement. Leave out pay amounts.

notes.b: Employees can now take time off for children, illness and holidays without losing all of their income.
points: Statutory paid annual leave means every employee is entitled to paid holidays, which is why family holidays became regular.
Maternity leave and maternity benefit come under the Maternity Protection Acts 1994 and 2004, so a mother can take time off for childbirth without losing all of her income.
Paternity leave comes under the Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016 and lasts two weeks, so a father can be at home after the birth.

Parental leave under the Parental Leave Act 1998 is unpaid time off to care for a child, while Parent's Leave and Benefit under the Parent's Leave and Benefit Act 2019 gives each parent leave with a benefit payment.
Statutory sick leave under the Sick Leave Act 2022 lets employees take paid time off for illness: 3 days in 2023, 5 in 2024, 7 in 2025 and 10 days a year from 2026.
Time off for children and illness lets parents care for their families without losing all their income.
notes.tip: Exam questions on improved conditions ask for items such as paid leave, sick pay, maternity and parental leave, so learn the Act that goes with each. Do not give weeks or euro amounts, apart from the two weeks of paternity leave.

notes.h: Security, safety and representation at work
notes.b: Alongside pay and leave, employees gained legal protection against unsafe workplaces and unfair treatment, and a way to bargain together.
points: Employees are entitled to written terms of employment, so both sides know the job, pay and conditions.
The Unfair Dismissals Acts protect employees from being dismissed without a fair reason, and redundancy payments compensate workers whose jobs are cut.

The Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 requires employers to provide a safe workplace and reduce the risk of workplace injury, and the Health and Safety Authority enforces it. Healthier, safer work lowers the risk of injury that would cut family income.

Grievance and disciplinary procedures give employees a route to challenge poor treatment or unfair conditions, and complaints can be taken to the Workplace Relations Commission, which hears employment complaints.
The Protection of Young Persons (Employment) Act 1996 is a law that protects young workers.

Trade unions negotiate pay and conditions on behalf of their members through collective agreements (agreements between unions and employers covering a group of workers). ICTU is the national body for Irish trade unions.
notes.tip: A question asking for two rights an employee has under law is easy marks: name an Act and say what it gives, for example the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 and a safe workplace.

notes.b: Some of the biggest gains for families are not in the weekly pay packet but in the benefits that come with a job.
points: Occupational pension schemes (pensions arranged through an employer) provide retirement income, reducing the need for adult children to support retired parents.
The My Future Fund scheme began on 1 January 2026 and automatically enrols employees aged 23 to 60 who earn over EUR 20,000, so more workers build up a pension.
In My Future Fund the employee, the employer and the State all contribute, which means the worker does not carry the whole cost.
Other benefits of a job can include canteens, health insurance, bonuses, training and career breaks.

notes.h: Effects of changes in work on family life
notes.b: Taken together, shorter hours, more leisure and better pay and conditions have changed family life, with benefits and strains.
points: Higher incomes let families move to larger or better housing and buy household goods.
Reduced hours and more leisure can strengthen family relationships through shared activities.
Long hours or shift work can cause tiredness and strain, and reduce time spent with children.
When both parents work full-time, there may be less time for family meals and supervision of children.
notes.tip: Shift work and part-time work change the pattern of hours; they are not themselves 'better conditions'. State clearly which effects are positive and which negative, and link each to the family. For flexible working at Higher Level, mention problems such as lower pay, fewer promotions and a blurred boundary between work and home.

notes.h: Practical setting: family life then and now
notes.b: Comparing family life a hundred years ago with today shows the changes in work directly. An interview with an older relative gives first-hand evidence.
points: Interview an older relative about the hours worked each week, the holidays taken each year and the leisure activities they had as a young adult.
Record the same three measures for a present-day family and note the differences in working hours, holidays and leisure.
Compare the two answers to show how changes in work have altered who has time for leisure and when it is taken.

keyTerms.definition: The number of hours regarded as a normal full-time week, which has shortened over time.
An arrangement that lets employees choose their start and finish times within agreed limits.
Working set periods at different times of day or night so that a workplace operates over extended hours.
The paid holiday entitlement that an employee earns each year.
Time not spent on paid work, household duties or personal care, used for recreation.
Income left after tax and essential deductions, available for spending or saving.
The lowest hourly rate of pay that an employer is legally allowed to pay a worker.
The terms under which people work, including hours, breaks, leave, safety and sick pay.
An organisation of workers that negotiates pay and conditions on behalf of its members.

factCards.term: Four home entertainment media that changed family leisure
factCards.definition: Television, radio, the home computer and the internet.

factCards.term: Three benefits of a shorter working week for family life
factCards.definition: More time for shared meals, more time for children's homework and activities, and more time for household tasks.

factCards.term: Two legal protections on working hours
factCards.definition: A maximum average working week and mandatory rest breaks.

factCards.term: Four features of improved conditions of work
factCards.definition: Sick pay, maternity leave, occupational pensions and safe working conditions.

questions.prompt: Name two ways in which shorter working hours have changed family life in Ireland.
questions.model: More time for shared family meals and activities. More time for children's homework, sport and leisure. More time for household tasks and for caring for older relatives.

questions.prompt: Explain how improvements in pay and conditions of work, together with reduced working hours, have changed leisure patterns and relationships within families. Refer to at least one named support or legal protection in your answer.
questions.model: Reduced hours and paid annual leave created regular blocks of free time, so family holidays, weekend outings and shared activities became routine. Labour-saving appliances released time from housework for leisure. Rising real pay and disposable income allowed families to spend on sport, cinema, holidays and eating out, and to buy homes and goods that changed family routines. Pay protections such as a statutory national minimum wage, sick pay and maternity leave give security, reducing financial stress that strains relationships. Health and safety protections and grievance procedures reduce risk and give recourse for poor treatment. Shift work and long hours can still reduce time together, so families must plan joint activities. Home entertainment has increased indoor leisure, while community clubs offer shared activities outside the home.
